original_value: AbstractThe importance of social components of health has been emphasized both in epidemiology and public health. This paper highlights the significant impact of social components on health outcomes in a novel way. Introducing the concept of sociomarkers, which are measurable indicators of social conditions in which a patient is embedded, we employed a machine learning approach that uses both biomarkers and sociomarkers to identify asthma patients at risk of a hospital revisit after an initial visit with an accuracy of 66%. The analysis has been performed over an integrated dataset consisting of individual-level patient information such as gender, race, insurance type, and age, along with ZIP code-level sociomarkers such as poverty level, blight prevalence, and housing quality. Using this uniquely integrated database, we then compare the traditional biomarker-based risk model and the sociomarker-based risk model. A biomarker-based predictive model yields an accuracy of 65% and the sociomarker-based model predicts with an accuracy of 61%. Without knowing specific symptom-related features, the sociomarker-based model can correctly predict two out of three patients at risk. We systematically show that sociomarkers play an important role in predicting health outcomes at the individual level in pediatric asthma cases. Additionally, by merging multiple data sources with detailed neighborhood-level data, we directly measure the importance of residential conditions for predicting individual health outcomes.

result.paraphrase: Abstract: The role of social determinants of health has been highlighted in both epidemiology and public health. This paper presents their effect on health outcomes in a new way. We introduce sociomarkers, measurable indicators of the social conditions surrounding a patient, and use a machine-learning method combining biomarkers and sociomarkers to identify asthma patients likely to return to the hospital after an initial visit with 66% accuracy. The analysis uses an integrated dataset that includes individual patient data such as gender, race, insurance type, and age, together with ZIP code-level sociomarkers including poverty level, blight prevalence, and housing quality. Using this integrated database, we compare a conventional biomarker-based risk model with a sociomarker-based risk model. The biomarker-based model achieves 65% accuracy, while the sociomarker-based model predicts with 61% accuracy. Even without specific symptom-related features, the sociomarker-based model can correctly identify two out of three at-risk patients. We systematically demonstrate that sociomarkers are important for predicting individual-level health outcomes in pediatric asthma cases. In addition, by combining multiple data sources with detailed neighborhood-level information, we directly quantify the importance of residential conditions in predicting individual health outcomes.
